Brands are piggybacking off the potential sales that targeting millions of ardent followers can bring – but there are risks

F rom the Avon ladies to the former Sex Pistols lead singer John Lydon selling butter , personal endorsement of products is a well-trodden form of marketing with significant gains – and pitfalls. More recently, the practice of teaming up with social media influencers has become a boom in the ad industry over the last decade – and came firmly into the spotlight this week.

First, the Guardian revealed that Unilever, the consumer goods behemoth behind huge brands including Dove soap to Hellmann’s mayonnaise, had slashed its almost £100m TV ad budget and was ploughing funds into online influencer marketing instead.

Then, a furore broke out over Andy Burnham’s interview with a TikToker, which involved filming a parody of Hugh Grant’s famous Love Actually dance inside 10 Downing Street.

The attempt to burnish Brand Burnham was further tarnished when it emerged that two more influencers, who had been invited to events at the prime minister’s residence, had posted clips filmed on the steps of No 10 featuring lewd, explicit or inappropriate lyrics .

The incident reignited the debate about the risks of tapping the “wild west” of online influencers and content creators in order to reach younger audiences increasingly trading TV for social media channels.

Burnham has said he will not apologise for his headlong rush to embrace influencers to reach young audiences – a government spokesperson meekly explained that content creators are “obviously responsible” for what they post – but the fallout is a stark reminder of the potential problems.

Nevertheless, brands big and small are piggybacking off the potential sales that can be drummed up by targeting the millions of ardent fans of influencers.

By the end of the decade more than $9bn (£6.9bn) will be spent on the so-called creator economy, more than brands will spend on running ads on traditional TV and streaming services, according to the consultancy Madison and Wall.

“The oldest marketing strategy of all time is human advocacy and recommendation,” says Jessica Tamsedge, the chief executive of the ad agency Dentsu Creative UK and Ireland. “Whether it is the Avon lady or celebrity endorsement … now it is about the different types of voices that are enlisted to do different jobs for businesses and brands. However, that doesn’t mean using them is automatically good marketing.

“When you go into a creator-led strategy there is enormous variation between successful and unsuccessful campaigns.”

Earlier this month, Space NK faced a consumer backlash for organising a trip for celebrities and influencers, including Stacey Solomon and Alison Hammond, to the five-star country house hotel in Surrey to launch the beauty product retailer’s festive range.

Consumers criticised the luxury staycation – which included beauty treatments, hair and makeup by brands including YSL and GHD and a lavish Christmas party – as being “tone deaf” given the pressure on consumers’ finances, particularly as the festive period piles pressure on budgets.

Nevertheless, it can be argued that the risk of getting it wrong can potentially be far outweighed by the reward of getting right.

In May, Kathryn Turner, the director of product development at M&S Food, started posting on her own TikTok with about 30 followers and a couple of young staff supporting her.

She has quickly become a viral sensation - Marks & Spencer’s gen-Z marketing dream – with about 700,000 followers across TikTok and Instagram.

A video released this month in which Turner championed a new chocolate and cornflake cookie, prompted long queues and Covid-style scenes of panic buying as people rushed to bakery counters at some M&S stores.

Meanwhile, Unilever said this week it had upped its network of influencers and creators to more than 500,000, an almost seven-fold increase in two years.

When Fernando Fernandez took over as chief executive in March last year he said he wanted “an influencer in every zip code in the globe”, a strategy that has completely upended how the Anglo-Dutch company spends its €8bn (£6.7bn) annual marketing budget.

In the UK, where Unilever has historically been a top-three TV advertiser, it has more than halved its budget, including almost completely disappearing from Channel 4 , one of the country’s biggest broadcasters. Unilever’s partners have included the former Love Island contestant Molly-Mae Hague on laundry detergent and fabric conditioner brands and the beauty creator Jen Chae.

Understandably, the TV industry is up in arms about the idea that running ads in The Great British Bake Off and I’m A Celebrity… Get Me Out Of Here! may no longer be the best use of marketing spend.

“TV advertising is the decision that makes other marketing decisions better,” says Lindsey Clay, the chief executive of Thinkbox, the marketing body for commercial TV in the UK. “Advertisers shouldn’t sacrifice what works hardest for what feels newest. Not every advertiser is following the evidence.

“If they were, TV would be the last place they’d cut to fund influencers. Influencers clearly have their place, but shifting money from TV to fund them is self-defeating.”

Despite the occasional misfire, the influencer and creator market has rapidly matured, according to the Influencer Marketing Trade Body (IMTB), which was set up to professionalise the industry in 2021. That was the year that the UK ad watchdog “named and shamed” reality TV stars for repeatedly failing to tell followers when they were paid to promote products in posts.…

items.title: The hill I will die on: Cheques are still the best way to pay for things | Claire Jackson
items.author: Claire Jackson
items.content:
A debit card might be quicker and easier, but there are thrills big and small to be had from whipping out your chequebook

It often takes other people to identify your quirks. Mine is writing cheques, a fact I was made aware of recently by a younger colleague, who watched with bemusement as I filled one out. He’d never seen a chequebook in the wild, he explained, with the air of a naturalist encountering a rare species. He looked on as I, a millennial, wrote “one hundred and forty-one pounds and thirty pence only”, that last word thrilling in its assertiveness – I will pay my bill, South East Water, and not a penny more!

Having examined the whole procedure, including my procuring a stamp and envelope to send it off, he concluded – as so many have – that the process would be far better executed online. A friend also politely fed back that, although she appreciates how I “enclose a cheque” in every birthday card to her daughter, could I perhaps just do a bank transfer like everyone else?

Claire Jackson is a journalist who writes about classical music, art and animals

I t often takes other people to identify your quirks. Mine is writing cheques, a fact I was made aware of recently by a younger colleague, who watched with bemusement as I filled one out. He’d never seen a chequebook in the wild, he explained, with the air of a naturalist encountering a rare species. He looked on as I, a millennial, wrote “one hundred and forty-one pounds and thirty pence only”, that last word thrilling in its assertiveness – I will pay my bill, South East Water, and not a penny more!

Having examined the whole procedure, including my procuring a stamp and envelope to send it off, he concluded – as so many have – that the process would be far better executed online. A friend also politely fed back that, although she appreciates how I “enclose a cheque” in every birthday card to her daughter, could I perhaps just do a bank transfer like everyone else?

While many aspects of the 1990s have resurfaced – baggy jeans, Nirvana T-shirts and casual sexism – the cheque is viewed with the same disdain as dial-up internet. But I maintain that, if you must pay for something, it is truly the ideal way.

First, scribbling – holding a pen or pencil and feeling it move across the page – is enjoyable. Paying via cheque thus becomes a simple pleasure – selecting the correct ink (anything other than blue or black is frowned upon; graphite is completely unacceptable), and signing with a writing instrument rather than a finger.

Financial transactions can also be hasty – something I realised after finding myself in debt. While I now (grudgingly) have a contactless card, I still fear I might tap without checking the amount and lose a fortune. That would never happen with a cheque.

Inherent trust is required in accepting a cheque, which adds to its affability. One of my favourite pubs, The Harrow Inn in Steep, Hampshire , politely warns: “We do not take credit or debit cards. Cash and cheques are welcome.” I discovered this on a day I had neither, and the owner happily served me lunch on the understanding that a cheque would be sent in the post forthwith (it was). Even when such goodwill is manipulated, the act is described with characteristically charming language – case in point, cheques “bouncing”.

Of course, there are benefits to digital banking, some of them unexpected. A friend’s young son has a Monzo account for his pocket money. Having ushered him away from the sweets being sold onboard as they were disembarking a Thames Clipper, she became occupied with her other child. When she looked up, her son had disappeared. Just as the boat slipped its moorings, her phone buzzed with a Monzo update that her son had just bought the contraband snacks – realising where he had gone, her family was swiftly united.

But this lady’s not for turning. I recently got a letter from HMRC informing me that I had overpaid my tax, and outlining the ways in which I might receive my refund. I don’t think I need to tell you which option I selected.

Claire Jackson is a journalist who writes about classical music, art and animals

items.lbText:
Meta claims its Muse assistant will make users’ lives easier, but business owners say AI is driving them to go analogue

R estaurant owners are battling a horde of AI bots and returning to using the telephone instead of online booking as new virtual assistants launch in the UK – but sometimes even that isn’t enough to stop them.

This week, Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta launched its Muse AI assistant in the UK and is encouraging users to let it shop and make restaurant reservations. The bot is given access to the user’s email if they give it permission, and it can make restaurant bookings and go shopping on the user’s behalf.

Muse has been downloaded millions of times in the US, but it has caused chaos for restaurants. The online booking platform Resy has banned bots after restaurants on the platform were swarmed with agents that can refresh the page thousands of times and snap up all the reservations. Now, AI agents are plaguing venues in the UK.

Dave Strauss, the co-owner of Bouchon Racine, which was recently crowned UK restaurant of the year , said he had already had an argument with a would-be diner’s AI bot.

He answers the phones in his French restaurant every day from 11am to take reservation requests and said recently he received an unnerving call: “The other day I answered the phone to an AI bot that sounded very realistic. There was something a bit wrong about it – it sounded exactly like a human being, but something was off. I asked if it was a bot and it said: ‘Yes this is an AI booking process.’”

Strauss added: “I had an argument with the AI bot and told it to never call me again. But that wasn’t very satisfying as it didn’t argue back.”

Kimberley Coke, a high-end restaurant concierge, is paid by celebrities to secure a good table at top dining spots. She said she was worried about the swarm of AI bots: “I think it is terrifying and it could cause absolute chaos.”

Coke, who makes all her bookings via WhatsApp or phone calls, added: “There is now so much information you can get online about the hottest restaurants and where to go, and it is really hard to get the tables and that is why people come to me as I have personal relationships with the restaurants. With the apps, you don’t know who the client is, you have no background on who is coming in, they still might not show up. There is nothing worse for a restaurant in December when they have empty tables.”

Meta has claimed that its product can make people’s lives easier, but that has not been the case for the restaurants on the receiving end of the calls, emails and reservation app bookings.

The problem has been pronounced in New York City, where hard-to-secure restaurant tables are a status symbol. One of the most popular is 4 Charles Prime Rib, which serves a famous double wagyu cheeseburger, often served topped with a fried egg. It has been a popular target for AI agents, with sources at Resy saying they were having to ban multiple accounts using bots to book reservations there.

Strauss said: “There has been a constant shift to make everything as automated as possible to save a bit of money. We believe here that doesn’t work. We get a lot of emails now saying we can outsource our bookings and phone calls to AI. That makes us more keen on doing it the way that we do it. If I could get rid of online booking, I would.”

Jeremy King, who owns Simpson’s in the Strand , Arlington and the Park, said that the move towards depersonalising interactions by using AI was making him go “more analogue” in his restaurants – diners will find it much easier to snag a prime table at one of his venues by picking up the phone.

He said: “I am very happy to embrace new technology but ultimately if it conspires against us we will have to return to managing without.”

Such agents are likely to become more common in the UK and Meta has deals with an array of British businesses – including Marks & Spencer, Currys, Sainsbury’s and easyJet – allowing Muse to navigate their websites more easily and to access their apps. If a company does not offer a “connector” app that Muse can visit, the agent will access its website instead.

The Information Commissioner’s Office and the Competition and Markets Authority said they had been in talks with Meta before Muse’s launch about its responsibility to comply with UK laws. The ICO, the UK’s data protection watchdog, said on Tuesday the tech company had committed to a “voluntary monitoring and reporting scheme”, while the CMA said talks had resulted in changes to make the app’s terms and conditions fairer

items.lbText:
Residents woke up to find their vital box missing, but despite 11 months of lobbying the company now says it cannot replace it

Residents of a remote Devon village now have to drive more than a mile to send letters after their attempts to get a new postbox literally hit the rocks.

Villagers in North Huish have described a farcical near 11-month battle to challenge Royal Mail’s excuses after their box vanished without warning last January.

Royal Mail has now informed them the box will not be replaced because the ground is too stony.

The residents fear that their vanishing postbox is part of a move by Royal Mail to reduce collections.

A number of communities have complained that their postal deliveries have been cut after the regulator Ofcom relaxed Royal Mail’s performance targets last year. Ofcom is now investigating claims that parcel deliveries are being prioritised over letters after nearly a quarter of first-class mail failed to arrive on time.

The saga started in January when Royal Mail claimed that the box had been found on the ground and was beyond repair as its supporting post had rotted.

After initially agreeing to replace it after villagers’ complaints, it incorrectly claimed that the site was privately owned and it could not proceed.

It subsequently blamed a council administration fee, and then a nearby parking area, for preventing reinstatement, before announcing that loose stones on the site made installation impossible.

North Huish parish council offered to buy the postbox-sized plot of land to speed up the process, and a local farmer has volunteered to install a new supporting post, but Royal Mail has refused to budge. “We initially thought the box had been stolen when it suddenly went missing,” says North Huish resident Lesley Ring.

“It was used regularly and none of us had ever noticed that it was unstable. In the light of subsequent events, we think Royal Mail just came and took it.”

Royal Mail initially told villagers that the replacement process would take up to four months.

“It cited the need for breaking ground permits, permission from landowners, compliance checks, underground utility checks and health and safety checks,” Ring says.

“We were extremely surprised at the apparent red tape involved and, over the following months, Royal Mail seemed to gradually go back on its word and came up with a variety of obstacles.”

In August, residents were told all options had been exhausted because the site of the original box, alongside a public telephone kiosk, was privately owned and no alternatives could be found.

Royal Mail declined to check ownership of the plot because it would have to pay Devon county council a £72 search fee for the service, and it declared the case closed.

The council agreed to perform the search for free to break the impasse, and confirmed that the plot was on a public highway.

Royal Mail then declared that loose stones and uneven ground had forced it to cancel the project.

Villagers were told that they could hand any letters for posting to their postal worker during a delivery round, provided there was capacity to carry it.

“We rarely see a postman as we tend to get post in one or two bundles a week,” says Ring. “The nearest box is over half an hour’s walk away, which puts it out of reach of elderly and disabled people who can’t drive.”

Ring says service failures are affecting her long-distance relationship. “My partner and I have conducted our relationship largely by post for 27 years, and we write to each other constantly, with a phone call on a Sunday,” she says.

“Too often recently, the conversation is hampered by the fact that letters have been held up from week to week, despite the fact that we only use so-called first-class post.”

Royal Mail says: “We understand how important it is for residents in North Huish to be able to post letters close to home, and we’re sorry we haven’t been able to replace the village postbox.

“The old box fell when the wooden post supporting it rotted. We planned to put a replacement in the same spot, but our engineer found that the uneven ground and damaged kerb raised safety concerns.

“We looked at other locations nearby but couldn’t find a safe, accessible spot on public land.”

Royal Mail told us that “there are alternatives at Beneckowle, about three-quarters of a mile from the old site, and at Diptford, about a mile away”.

When the Guardian checked these distances using route planners, this indicated both of these locations were about a 1.3-mile drive away.

“We recognise that neither is as convenient as having a postbox in the village, so we’re also arranging for residents to be able to hand stamped letters to their postie when they receive a delivery,” it adds.

items.title: Grand Theft Anthropic: how GTA can inspire a fightback against AI | Alexander Hurst
items.author: Alexander Hurst
items.content:
Tech billionaires are taking us for a ride. But new ‘poison pill’ software could help shield human-made creative output from hijacking

Grand Theft Auto VI came out on the same day that Anthropic made its stock market debut. I keep thinking about that coincidence. As more than one tech writer has pointed out, the new GTA took 13 years to make, more than $1bn of investment and involved 9,000 sets of human hands, and it will probably be the last blockbuster video game to be fully free of generative AI.

On the day of its release, a group chat with my most gaming-minded male friends erupted in discussion about whether or not video games, and GTA VI specifically, rose to the level of art. Exploring a national park? Yes, that’s there. Badly assemble a coffee table from “Krapea” (the game’s fictional furniture company)? Ditto. Eating a hot dog? Why not. All of it gloriously human in origin. Perhaps that in itself is an argument for how GTA VI crosses the blurry line from entertainment to something more. It is a medium by which human beings offer others a (necessarily incomplete) interpretation of what it’s like to be them in the world, or to try to transcend it.

Alexander Hurst writes for Guardian Europe from Paris

items.title: ‘The key is pricing realistically’: how to sell your home in a falling market
items.author: Sandra Haurant
items.content:
From small fixes such as decluttering to taking your property off the market for a break, there are ways to seal the deal

Selling your home is always a big task, but when the headlines are telling you prices are falling, it can feel even more daunting.

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
From small fixes such as decluttering to taking your property off the market for a break, there are ways to seal the deal

Selling your home is always a big task, but when the headlines are telling you prices are falling, it can feel even more daunting.

Average house prices in the UK fell by 1.2% over the year to 31 October, according to Lloyds bank – the steepest drop since late 2023.

Plus there are fewer people buying: in September, mortgage approvals for house purchase were down by 19.4% year on year, the most recent official data shows.

So just how worried should sellers be? “It is most certainly getting more difficult to sell a property in the UK,” says Stuart Ducker, the strategic solutions director at the property data company TwentyCi.

Of the homes on market between January and October this year, 53.5% have been sold so far, Ducker says.

“But there are areas of the country – for example, inner London – where the chances of a sale are only 30%.

“In terms of property types, the flats market is not great at the minute: the likelihood of selling a flat nationally is only 41% in 2026 to date.”

House prices in Greater London are down by 3.1% year on year, according to the latest Lloyds data, while south-east and south-west England have recorded falls of 2.4% over the year.

But in some other parts of the UK, prices have been going up, albeit more slowly than before. Northern Ireland, for example, experienced average property values rising by 4.4% in the year to the end of October.

And within regions it is a mixed picture. “Even in some of those more challenging parts of the market, there are still areas where there’s a shortage of stock,” says Emily Williams, the director of research at Savills estate agents.

She adds: “In outer London there’s still decent demand that has not been met by good available stock for family housing. So, if you’ve got a good family house, there are still buyers out there looking.”

Things could be more problematic if you are selling your home in the south of England and buying a new home in a region where prices are still rising, as your buying power may be reduced.

Others who stand to lose out when prices fall are sellers who do not plan to buy another property, or downsizers who are relying on a set amount of equity to fund their retirement, or help family members.

However, for those moving within the same region, a fall might work in their favour.

“What matters is the gap between the home being sold and the home being bought, not the headline price of either,” says Nick Mendes, the technical manager at the mortgage broker John Charcol. “Those trading up are often in the strongest position when prices are softening.”

Whatever your situation and wherever you are in the country, finding a buyer quickly depends on getting the price right.

It is most important to price “realistically” at the outset, Williams says. “Buyers are very savvy. Everyone can look at Rightmove or Zoopla and see what things have sold for previously.”

The trouble is, it can be very difficult to know what the right price is. Typically, a seller might ask three or four estate agents to come and value their home – but they may all come up with different valuations that vary by many thousands of pounds.

As well as checking recently sold properties in your area, on portals such as Rightmove and Zoopla, it is also worth challenging the agents to justify their valuations.

Alex Oppenheim, a director at John D Wood estate agents, says: “Ask the agents to show their recent comparable evidence. Can they show you similar properties that they have actually sold in that price range in the past few months?”

Agents might say they have buyers looking for a property similar to yours, and it is perfectly possible to test the waters.

Oppenheim says: “You can agree for them to market your property to those buyers, without putting it on the portals to begin with, to see if there is any interest. You can even say, ‘If you get a buyer at that figure, I will give you an extra 0.5%’.”

Then, if that doesn’t work, you can think about listing the property for sale with a lower price.

It can be demoralising to have a stream of viewers coming through the door and no offers. It could be easy to think there is something wrong with the property. Perhaps if you repainted, or changed the carpets, or did something with the kitchen, it might help? Oppenheim suggests that is rarely the solution.

But there may be some simple things you can do to make a difference.

Creating a sense of light and space by clearing away clutter and cleaning the windows is always a good idea, as is generally maintaining the property even when you are trying to sell it.

“I would recommend spending on things that fall under the category of maintenance. So if, for example, you have repaired a leak and there is still some evidence of the old damage on the ceiling, you should absolutely get that repainted,” Oppenheim says.

“But you could spend thousands on cosmetic changes, and it will probably make no difference. There is a misconception about problems with properties languishing on the market for a long time without finding a buyer. There is typically nothing wrong with those properties – the only thing that is wrong is the price.”

Sam Molyneux-Summers, the chief operating officer at the estate agents Century 21, says buyers dictate the market.

“We always ask for feedback after viewings, including what people think about the price,” he says. “If we are consistently hearing that people think it is too high, we will suggest lowering it.”

The problem is that lowering it can, in itself, make it harder to sell. Research from Savills, which focused on houses with asking prices above £1m, shows that where a property did not need a price cut, it took about eight weeks to sell. Where there was at least one cut, it took about 13 weeks longer. And if you needed two or more, it took an additional 16 weeks.…

The Christmas staple is smaller this year after a hot, dry summer hit the water-loving – but versatile – brassica

They are a key ingredient in many Christmas dinners, but brussels sprouts appearing on diners’ plates this festive season are likely to be smaller than usual, after the hot, dry summer took its toll on the water-loving crop.

Sprouts are generally planted outdoors between March and early June, meaning they were already in the ground when the UK faced a series of heatwaves and drought conditions across Wales and most of England.

Low water-reserves limited the amount growers could use to irrigate their crops, slowing down the growth of sprouts and other brassica such as cabbages, broccoli and cauliflowers.

Sprouts grow on a stalk, maturing from the bottom upwards. This means the largest sprouts are found at the bottom, with the smallest at the top. Supermarkets and other food retailers generally select only the mid-sized sprouts, found in the middle.

Higher volumes of stunted sprouts are available this year after a challenging growing season, according to the low-waste food retailer Oddbox, which is known for supplying wonky fruit and vegetables.

“We would typically see smaller sprouts heading to Oddbox, because that’s the product that growers don’t tend to have outlets for, but this year there’s an awful lot more of them,” said Gavin Phelps, the company’s head of sourcing.

Most of the sprouts available are from Lincolnshire, where quantities of brassica and other crops are grown, but which has had extended periods of drought.

Some consumers may believe that smaller sprouts will be harder to peel than larger ones, making the much-maligned vegetable more difficult to prepare.

Phelps said this was not the case: “Peeling small sprouts is of course going to be a bit of extra effort, but you can also save some prep time because you don’t need to cut them in half like you typically do with the larger size ones. So it equals out.”

Sprouts are harvested in the UK between September and March, although a quarter of their annual consumption takes place in the two weeks leading up to Christmas.

Growers say that tweaks to sprout breeding and the introduction of new varieties have made the vegetable – sometimes criticised for perceived bitterness – tastier. More than half of adults (56.4%) polled by YouGov in October said they liked sprouts , while the number who said they disliked them has fallen from 26% to under 22% in the past six years.

Cooking techniques have also improved, said Phelps. “Back 20 or 30 years ago there was this obsession with boiling everything. I feel people have come round to them more because there is just so much more out there in terms of recipe inspiration.”

Cooks may want to try roasting, pickling or even smashing sprouts this Christmas, while Phelps is planning to crisp his in an air fryer.

items.lbText:
Experts suggest AI companies may be sitting on ‘bombshell’ that could have severe consequences for secret information

Leading experts and the governor of the Bank of England have suggested that top AI companies might have something under their hat – a “bombshell” revelation about encryption. Depending on what it is, it could have major consequences for the world’s secret information, and the banks and governments that hold and transmit it.

This is because of recent, startling mathematical advances made by AI models, which are still being understood.

Some of the problems that have been solved relate to cryptography. Some are significant and have been the subject of entire careers.

Leading computer scientists think that, if AI has broken ground on these problems, it is overwhelmingly likely it has, or will soon, produce revelations about the core mathematics behind encoding the world’s information.

Scott Aaronson, a preeminent computer scientist, cited a recent proof – from Anthropic and OpenAI – that VP≠VNP, a finding that he says has led him to drink uncharacteristic amounts of wine in his kitchen.

In basic terms, this proof is about what problems can be solved easily by the computers we have, and what problems are truly “hard” problems – meaning that the world’s most powerful computers could not solve them in, say, a lifetime.

Theoretical computer scientists are interested in this question: are all problems in the world quickly solvable with good enough algorithms, or are there problems that might take vast amounts of time to solve, and for which no shortcuts are possible?

Anthropic and OpenAI’s proof that VP≠VNP is a major step forward in answering this question, which was first posed in the 1970s. While it concerns a slightly different problem from breaking encryption, it suggests that AI models can work ably in this territory and produce groundbreaking results.

The world was abuzz over the summer with claims new, powerful AI models – such as Mythos – were capable of finding hundreds of vulnerabilities in lines of code.

Put one way, this amounts to finding lots of grammatical errors in the language of computers. It isn’t particularly difficult, but artificial intelligence can do it well. AI can also help cyber-attackers find these errors and exploit them.

Breaking encryption is a far more fundamental challenge. It means making a novel mathematical discovery, which stands to illuminate our conceptual understanding of how computers work.

Encryption is based on the idea that some maths problems are too “hard” for computers to break, no matter how many GPUs you shove into a datacentre. But this is a very abstract thing to argue.

Governments, banks and tech companies have been updating the encryption they use in anticipation of powerful quantum computers coming online. Their new methods – or old methods – may be resilient to decryption algorithms.

If they were not resilient, and a decryption algorithm were discovered, that algorithm could still be difficult to implement in practice.

Still, the extreme scenario is vast amounts of information, from Swift bank transfers to the private messages of government officials could suddenly be read by those who could access it. This could include secure exchanges from decades ago.

Many intelligence agencies put listening devices on cables to collect information transmitted through them. One example is GCHQ. Such agencies may not have been able to crack this information up to now, but that could suddenly change.

Exclusive: AI may have cracked decades-old maths problems that underpin encryption at banks and government agencies

AI companies are sitting on “bombshell” revelations that could disrupt a cornerstone of security for banks and governments in as soon as a few months, leading experts believe.

Scott Aaronson, a pre-eminent theoretical computer scientist, told the Guardian there were “well-attested rumours” that powerful artificial intelligence models had broken ground on decades-old maths problems related to how the world encodes secret information.

Depending on what has been discovered, it is possible that hackers – and many other people – could in short order have the power to more easily decrypt the world’s secret communications: banking transactions, diplomatic cables and private emails, for example.

If this happened, then spy agencies, governments, banks and private companies could be forced to very suddenly update the foundations of how they communicate, or risk extremely sensitive information being widely exposed.

Aaronson’s and others’ concerns come from a series of mathematical advances that frontier AI companies have announced in the past weeks.

Most of these are abstract breakthroughs. But to experts in the field, they indicate that AI is powerful enough to crack problems that most of them thought would be unsolved for the foreseeable future.

Earlier this week, Aaronson wrote that he was “virtually certain, from multiple reliable sources, that the AI labs are now sitting on one or more bombshells [in cryptography]”.

“The people who thought AI couldn’t do any interesting maths are definitely wrong at this stage, and so it’s no longer clear where the limit is,” said Steven Murdoch, a professor of computer science at University College London.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4’s Today programme on Friday, the mathematician Marcus du Sautoy said “we don’t know” what the broader ramifications of many of these discoveries were, and what this meant for encryption.

But, he added, “no one has been talking about the problem which is at the heart of protecting all our electronic secrets. Why is nobody talking about that problem? Some of us are thinking: maybe they’ve already solved it, and of course, it would have such massive implications that everyone has just kept it quiet.”

Governments, banks and spy agencies have been preparing for the possibility of powerful decryption for the past few years. This is because quantum computers, when developed, will be able to break the decades-old algorithms that underpin many forms of encryption.

But the timeline for quantum computers to be able to do this is still years away, not weeks or months. Murdoch said many governments and technology companies were working towards a higher standard of encryption – one that would not be vulnerable to quantum computers – but slowly. “The target was something like 2032, and that was probably going to be missed.”

Now he, Aaronson and others think there may be sudden advances in what the world understands about cryptography, and these could come soon.

What these revelations could be is less certain. What Aaronson and others think could have happened is that either AI has come up with a new way to break encryption or, conversely, it has proved that such a shortcut does not exist.

This would come from AI models picking apart the maths that underlies encryption, and that up until this point has not been fully understood. If AI has done this, it could find a way to decrypt, and therefore expose, massive amounts of secret data.

It could also prove this information is more secure than previously thought.

The world uses multiple forms of encryption – based on different underlying algorithms – and there are different guesses as to what may have been found, and therefore what systems could be affected.

No concrete announcements have come from AI companies regarding revelations about encryption, said Aaronson, but “anyone informed is assuming” that they are there.

Alan Woodward, a professor of computer science at the University of Surrey, said a mathematical breakthrough related to cryptography would not necessarily mean widespread chaos tomorrow. What has changed is the speed at which AI is solving problems that have been shrouded in mystery for decades – with potentially serious consequences.

“What [Aaronson] is basically saying is that people need to be ready for something to suddenly spring out, because there’s definitely a sort of a trend.”

Earlier this week, Andrew Bailey, the governor of the Bank of England, addressed fears that companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic had achieved breakthroughs in cryptography, saying these companies should be cautious about releasing new models to the public.

In the past weeks, AI companies have released proofs of mathematical results that closely relate to this question. One of these involved a foundational question about how to categorise computationally “hard” problems.

Aaronson said these breakthroughs had been seismic for experts in the fields of maths and computer science, some of whom have spent their careers working on these problems, and others who assumed that these problems would not be solved in their lifetimes.

“We’ve never seen a period like this,” he said. “I’m trying to face the reality of what is happening.”

He emphasised that these breakthroughs still needed to be understood, however – which means human mathematicians and computer scientists need to go through and verify the proofs that AI companies say they have produced.

Woodward said it was unlikely that any discoveries would “undo encryption by the end of the week”. Even if such a finding exists, there are hurdles to its widespread deployment.

But big banks and governments that rely on encryption “need to be agile”, said Woodward. “The ones that are agile and can change quickly will be safe. The ones that are the laggards could get caught out.”

Anthropic and OpenAI were approached for comment.

Watchdog had found ‘repeated’ misconduct by veteran’s daughter and her husband in running the foundation

A charity set up by the family of the pandemic fundraiser Captain Sir Tom Moore has applied to be struck off.

The charity is now known as the 1189808 Foundation, having dropped Moore’s name at the request of his family last year.

An application to have the organisation struck off appeared on the Companies House register on Friday.

The dropping of the captain’s name came after the charities watchdog found there had been “repeated” misconduct and mismanagement on the part of the second world war veteran’s daughter and her husband in their running of the foundation.

The Charity Commission’s report published in 2024 found a “repeated pattern of behaviour” through which Hannah Ingram-Moore and her husband, Colin, made private gains and which the regulator said would have left people feeling “misled”.

The report found that a £1.4m book deal and an £18,000 awards ceremony appearance fee were among the financial benefits the Ingram-Moores enjoyed through their family links to the Captain Tom Foundation, which was launched in May 2020.

The Ingram-Moores have already been banned from being charity trustees, and Hannah Ingram-Moore was prohibited from being a trustee or holding a senior management role in any charity in England and Wales for 10 years, and Colin Ingram-Moore for eight years.

Moore became a household name during the first Covid-19 lockdown, raising £39.4m for NHS charities by walking laps of the garden at his home in Marston Moretaine, Bedfordshire. He was honoured with a knighthood from Queen Elizabeth II.

The millions raised and donated to NHS Charities Together for its Covid-19 Urgent Appeal before the foundation was formed were not part of the commission’s inquiry.

Moore, a father of two who was born in Keighley, West Yorkshire, died aged 100 in February 2021 after testing positive for coronavirus.

At this pivotal moment in American history, let us move forward together to take on and defeat a powerful, greedy and corrupt ruling class

W e are at a pivotal moment in history. Never before in human history have so few people held so much wealth and so much power. And never before have we seen such an unprecedented level of greed, arrogance and irresponsibility on the part of the world’s ruling class.

Here is the good news: leaders from around the world are finally starting to wake up. This week, elected officials and economists from around the world – including four Nobel prize winners – came together in Paris for a “Summit Against International Oligarchy”. As the summit’s proclamation stated, “The explosion of extreme wealth is the major social fact of our time … We are sounding the alarm: billionaires are a threat to our democracies.”

They are right. And that is exactly why I organized, along with other progressives, the Fight Oligarchy tour last year which brought out more than 340,000 Americans in 27 states.

As members of the summit point out, in 1987 the wealth of the richest 0.0001% amounted to the equivalent of 3% of global gross domestic product (GDP). Since then, these 3,000 households have seen their fortunes grow to 17% of global GDP.

At this moment, we live in a world where the top 1% owns more wealth than the bottom 95% of humanity and the gap between the very rich and the poor is growing wider and wider.

Think about it. After all of the wars and revolutions over the last 250 years, after all of the carefully drafted constitutions and hard-fought elections, after all of the wonderful speeches that politicians around the world have given, the top 1% owns more wealth than the bottom 95% of humanity.

In country after country, we are seeing unprecedented income and wealth inequality.

We see it in America today, where the top 1% now owns more wealth than the bottom 93% and one man, Elon Musk, owns more wealth than the bottom 53% of American households.

We see it in Russia, where the latest figures indicate that the wealthiest 500 people in that country control more wealth than the bottom 99.8% of their people.

We see it in France, where more than one out of five children live in poverty, while 53 billionaires own more wealth than the bottom half of the population.

We see it in Africa, where in recent years, nearly 850 million people have struggled with food insecurity, while just four men own more wealth than the bottom 50% of the people on that continent. Yes. Four men own more wealth than half a continent.

We see it in Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Qatar, where a handful of families have unbelievable wealth and power while most of the work done in those countries is performed by impoverished and powerless migrant laborers.

But it’s not just massive income and wealth inequality. It is oligarchs’ control over the global economy. It is oligarchs’ control over much of the media and what people see, hear and read. It is oligarchs avoiding taxes by stashing trillions of dollars in offshore tax havens around the world while the children in their native countries go hungry.

And what are the political implications when the very rich get much richer while working people struggle and feel more and more powerless?

The answer is clear. If people no longer believe that their government is responding to their needs, many of them will give up on democracy and move towards authoritarianism.

And it’s not just Trumpism in the United States. It’s the growth of extreme rightwing parties in Germany, France, the UK and elsewhere.

All over the world, people are asking a very simple question: why should I continue to vote for the same old, same old political parties when my job has been shipped overseas, my factory has been automated, my credit card interest rate is now 25%, I’m unable to retire with dignity, and my children will likely have a lower standard of living than I do – all while the top 1% have never, ever had it so good?

As the country the most billionaires, with a record 989, including 15 of the top 20, the US has a major role to play.

Bottom line: if we are going to improve the lives of working people and protect democracy, the new Democratic majority can no longer continue the failed status quo policies that have devastated so many of our people throughout our country.

This election was about change, real change, and that’s what Democrats must deliver. Now is the time to take on Big Money and fight for an economy that works for all, not just a few.

Yes. We need a wealth tax on billionaires to substantially reduce child poverty, build affordable housing, protect our seniors and invest in the needs of working families.

Yes. We need to guarantee healthcare as a human right by passing Medicare for All.

Yes. We must raise the minimum wage to a living wage – at least $20 an hour – and make it easier for workers to join unions by passing the Pro Act.

Yes. We must strengthen public education and make higher education available to all, regardless of income.

Yes. We must make sure that AI and robotics benefit working families and not just enrich a handful of big tech oligarchs.

Yes. We must ensure that everyone in America can retire with dignity by expanding social security, scrapping the cap on taxable income and restoring traditional defined benefit pension plans.

The new Democratic majority in Congress must act boldly and with an unprecedented sense of urgency. The crises facing our country and the world are much too dangerous to be ignored, or to be dealt with through tepid half-measures.

At this pivotal moment in American history, let us move forward together to take on and defeat a powerful, greedy and corrupt ruling class.

Bernie Sanders is a US senator, and ranking member of the health, education, labor and pensions committee. He represents the state of Vermont and is the longest-serving independent in the history of Congress

items.title: The Guardian view on AI and the Riemann hypothesis: a triumph of intelligence, a test of democracy | Editorial
items.author: Editorial
items.content:
Machines are solving problems that have been beyond the reach of human ingenuity. Their growing power must not become the sole preserve of billionaires

For the average person, the news that AI has helped crack a problem that has defied mathematicians since 1859 might elicit momentary awe. What ought to worry everyone is not the discovery per se, but what it says about the power of the machines making it. The pace of scientific discovery looks like it is outrunning the ability of humanity – and its institutions – to understand, let alone regulate, AI’s advances.

Last Friday Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, said that he, with the assistance of an unreleased version of the company’s Claude chatbot, had produced what many mathematicians see as the holy grail: a proof for the Riemann hypothesis. Mathematicians like Cornell University’s Steven Strogatz had already cried on podcasts, lamenting that students were asking: “What’s the point if the AI can do math better than any human being?” Computers can validate the Alpöge-Claude proof. But Prof Strogatz fears AI’s discoveries may soon defy human understanding. Asking AI to explain them, he said, would be like him trying to teach calculus to his own dog.

items.lbText:
Warning of ‘lights out for Labour in Scotland’ as Burnham faces choice between warring factions over North Sea drilling project

Dozens of Labour MPs in favour of Rosebank are putting pressure on the prime minister not to block the North Sea oilfield, warning that doing so could spell “lights out for Labour in Scotland”.

As many as 80 pro-drilling MPs are considering writing their own letter to Andy Burnham after nearly 100 of their colleagues called on the prime minister not to allow the project to proceed . Scottish Labour leader Michael Marra has also reiterated his support for Rosebank, cautioning that “working-class people in vocational jobs” were threatened by the decline of the North Sea basin.

Burnham now faces having to choose between two warring factions within his own party in what is likely to be the most sensitive decision he has taken so far as prime minister.

Anti-Rosebank MPs warn about the impact on the climate. They argue that the estimated additional 254m tonnes of carbon dioxide which Rosebank will produce over its lifetime are not worth the extra £500m in tax receipts and 500 jobs it will generate.

But those in favour of the project worry that a decision not to go ahead will damage Labour’s reputation with industry and Scottish voters in general.

One MP told the Guardian: “This is very much part of Scotland’s economy and supply chain, but crucially Scotland’s identity. It has become such a totemic issue that Labour will not be forgiven in Scotland if they don’t do this.”

The person added: “Andy needs to approve Rosebank or it’s lights out for Labour in Scotland.”

Marra said he recognised that the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, had a “different” decision compared to the Jackdaw gasfield , but backed the project because of the jobs and economic activity it would support.

“The decline of the North Sea may be seen as something to celebrate by those who want us to meet our climate obligations.

“I understand that. But I ask those who call for a just transition to understand the anxiety in Aberdeen and the north-east of Scotland over a political establishment which often feels to them that it considers anything but clean energy a dirty word.

“This is people’s lives and livelihoods we are talking about. Not the millionaire shareholders of a billion-dollar multinational, but working-class people in vocational jobs,” the Scottish Labour leader said.

Several MPs have sent individual letters to Burnham urging him to allow the project to go ahead, but many are now in talks about whether to coordinate their efforts to counteract a letter against Rosebank signed by nearly 100 of their collegaues.

One Labour MP said: “The whips and the government know we have the support, we’ve made that clear behind the scenes. Conversations [over a joint letter] are ongoing over the weekend.”

Another added: “Reindustrialisation and energy jobs for young people are huge issues in Scotland, so the feeling is they need to approve it to show we’re serious about it.”

Henry Tufnell, Labour MP for mid and south Pembrokeshire said: “Failing to approve Rosebank would cost industrial communities jobs and investment, weaken our balance of payments and deny the exchequer vital tax revenues.”

Torcuil Crichton, the Labour MP for Na h-Eileanan an Iar (Western Isles), said: “We need the workforce, the supply chain and the expertise of the North Sea to build our renewable future.

“There are now more jobs in renewables than in the carbon sector, but we can’t abandon the workforce like other energy communities were abandoned by the Tories.”

He told BBC Radio Scotland: “It makes far more sense from a domestic security point of view and an environmental point of view to source those carbon fuels within our own boundaries. If we don’t, we’re importing a huge carbon footprint from other places.

“So there’s no point outsourcing our environmental conscience.”

Burnham has enjoyed early success in office by uniting his previously fractious parliamentary party and winning back voters who had defected to other leftwing parties. The Rosebank decision, however, will test his ability to keep his fragile coalitions of MPs and voters together.

While Labour has enjoyed a poll bounce since Burnham became prime minister , the improvement has been more modest in Scotland and the party remains behind the Scottish National party.

In recent months, the SNP’s stance on oil and gas drilling in the North Sea has shifted. Once strong opponents of new projects under Nicola Sturgeon, the party abandoned its “presumption against” new North Sea projects in October. John Swinney has also criticised the UK government’s energy independence bill, which aims to ban new North Sea drilling.

Polling by Survation last month found that 64% of people in Scotland say that the UK government should approve Rosebank, with 16% against.

“In Scotland, the public supports approval for Rosebank in every age group excepted 18-to-24s. But even that is very close: there’s just a 1% net difference. According to our polling, allowing the project to go ahead would make Scottish voters more likely to vote Labour. Any route to a majority for Burnham hinges on Scottish seats,” said PJ Stock, a research and data analyst with Survation.

Emma Hardy, the environment minister, acknowledged on Friday morning that her party was split over the issue.

She told Sky News: “I know from chatting to some of my friends and colleagues, some Labour MPs in Scotland feel differently to some Labour MPs elsewhere. But I know Andy [Burnham], as our prime minister, will be listening to everybody.”

While Labour went into the last election promising not to issue any more North Sea oil and gas licences, they could give the environmental approval to this project – the largest undeveloped field in UK waters – because it already has a licence.…

Centrica boss memo to 400 workers at gas plant off Yorkshire coast says utility doing all it can ‘to save your jobs’

The boss of the British Gas owner Centrica has told hundreds of staff at its largest gas storage facility that he was seeking urgent talks with Andy Burnham and would do everything he could to save jobs.

Chris O’Shea, the chief executive of Centrica, reportedly told staff at the Rough gas storage facility off the east Yorkshire that the government had rebuffed the company’s plea for short-term support to run the store over the winter.

In a memo, seen by Sky News, O’Shea is understood to have expressed disappointment that the government had delayed its response to a consultation on whether to support the ageing underground gas stores over the longer term.

The Guardian understands that the government delivered its decision to Centrica in the last few weeks and the internal company memo was intended to update the facility’s staff about continuing talks.

The Rough gas storage facility supports about 400 jobs, including direct employees and contractors, but is scheduled to close at the end of March – unless the government intervenes – because it has become uneconomic to run.

Facilities typically store gas in the summer when the market price is lower, and sell it in winter when the price rises due to higher demand. But successive energy crises in recent years have upended this pattern, making it difficult to make enough money to invest in the upgrade work needed to keep the facility running.

“No decisions about roles have been made,” O’Shea wrote in the memo, according to Sky News. He reportedly added that the company was “doing everything we can to save your jobs” and that he would seek urgent talks with trade unions, Whitehall officials and the prime minister on the issue.

It is the latest in a series of warnings by Centrica over the future of the site. Centrica is listed on the FTSE 100, valued at nearly £7bn.

The jobs warning has emerged less than a fortnight after the energy company SSE told investors it would shut its Atwick gas storage site in east Yorkshire next summer unless the government offered support.

SSE said although the site continued to have “strategic importance” to the energy system as the North Sea’s domestic production declined, it was “increasingly clear” that the market would not support its continued operations.

Earlier this month, the National Energy System Operator (Neso) used a second consecutive annual report to warn that the UK was at risk of a gas supply crisis as the North Sea’s production wound down.

The report underlined concerns raised in Neso’s first annual report which found that while the UK has enough access to global gas markets to cover demand when weather is normal, if even a single piece of Britain’s ageing gas infrastructure suffered an “unlikely” outage during a very cold spell, then the UK could run out of gas.

A spokesperson for Centrica declined to comment.

items.lbText:
Norwegian airline tells customers not to come to airports after surging fuel costs caused by Iran war ruin finances

Norse Atlantic Airways has filed for bankruptcy and cancelled all future flights after surging fuel costs caused by the Iran war ruined its finances.

The Norwegian airline said it was entering insolvency and posted a message on its website telling customers not to come to airports – including passengers stranded away from home. Its collapse came a day after it put flights on hold with a warning that its finances were critical.

The carrier operated low-cost, long-haul flights around the world, including from London Gatwick and the US to Europe and Asia. Flights from Gatwick and Manchester next month to Thailand are among those now scrapped, along with London flights to South Africa and the US.

The Norse board concluded operations were no longer viable after a year in which airlines across the world were hit by spiralling oil prices that doubled the cost of jet fuel as well as dampening consumer demand, after the Iran war began in February.

Rival airlines have predicted surging air fares and the collapse of weaker carriers .

In a statement to the Oslo stock exchange, Eivind Roald, the chief executive of Norse, said: “The board of Norse Atlantic Airways AS has made the difficult decision to file for bankruptcy despite extensive efforts from the company and the group to find a solution.

“We are deeply sorry for the impact this has on our passengers, employees and partners.”

He said the owning group and Norse’s UK subsidiary – which was set up to comply with aviation rules after Brexit – were “working to find a solution for the remaining part of the business to continue operations”.

However, all UK flights were similarly cancelled and ticket sales halted.

In a message on its website, Norse advised passengers to contact their travel agents, flight bookers, insurers or credit card companies, but made clear those travelling were on their own and should ask airport information desks.

It said: “We know this will disrupt travel plans and may leave some passengers away from home. Customer service for both airlines is no longer available by phone, email, chat or social media.”

The abrupt end came after Norse announced it was on the brink of collapse on Thursday morning. On Friday morning, it reported that aircraft lessors had served termination notices for the 12 planes in its fleet.

Norse was founded in 2021, attempting to emulate the model of Norwegian Air , whose attempts to forge a new low-cost long-haul market ended with the pandemic.

Norse briefly revived the transatlantic routes using the same plane types, Boeing 787 Dreamliners.

However, it eventually hit similar financial turbulence and this summer told investors it was exploring a sale or merger, embarking on a $50m (£38m) cost-cutting programme, including shedding jobs and its Norwegian HQ.

items.lbText:
Department stores are hosting in-person events for those who find comfort in collecting the British soft toy brand

They’re cute, cuddly and taking over the homes of young adults.

Jellycat, a British soft toy brand founded in 1999, is experiencing a rise in interest from adult buyers as they snap up signature smiley designs in the shape of everything from croissants and disco balls to turtles and teabags.

The trend is part of a wider “kidult” movement, with grownups buying items traditionally geared towards children, for example, Lego sets and Pokémon cards . On social media, videos of users talking through their collections of soft toys known as plushies can rack up millions of views.

On Monday, Harrods in London is opening “a first-of-its-kind dining destination” – a Jellycat cafe serving brunch in edible and soft toy form. Diners will be able to buy a peach granola bowl-shaped plushie, and eat the dish too.

According to research by Circana, “kidult” toy sales in the UK grew 22% in the first half of 2026. One in five toys and games are now bought by over-18s for themselves. At the US department chain Nordstrom, the average age of a Jellycat buyer is 27. Everything from nostalgia to a rise in anxiety disorders is being credited as a contributing factor to the trend.

Audrey Tang, a chartered member of the British Psychological Society, describes Jellycats as “tactile, comforting, calming and very cutesy”. She isn’t surprised to see increased demand from adults for plushies. “This year has been tough on a lot of people so if there is anything that makes us smile or makes us feel nice, we’re probably going to choose that,” she says.

Tang dismisses age-regression concerns, saying it is a type of judgment. “Try thinking about where that voice about rules is coming from,” she says. “Often those types of judgments come from parents or caregivers who have previously told us: ‘You’re too old for this or you should grow out of that.’”

Each Jellycat “character” is given a name by the brand and a brief bio. The toys hover around the £20 to £40 mark but discontinued or rare versions can fetch upwards of £500 on secondhand sites. Jellycat ranked fourth among the UK’s most-searched terms between January and September 2026, eBay reports. The Jellycat boom has also led to a rise in reports of “stealing to sell” shoplifting .

Bill Nighy has described himself as a “big, big Jellycat customer”. Sarah Jessica Parker has posted a photo of her own “Petal” bunny, while Kylie Jenner’s Jellycat of choice is a trio of green peas in a pod.

Mini bag charms, including 6cm-high pickles and marshmallows, are increasingly being spotted swinging from designer handbags.

Booking for the Harrods Jellycat brunch, which takes over a space previously occupied by the Prada cafe, opened in October and slots are sold out until February.

Rachel Dyer, 43, a business support officer, has booked a table to celebrate her 10th wedding anniversary. Dyer, who started collecting Jellycats in 2025, now has 95 plushies including a pine-cone tree, a fox, and a cat wearing a parka jacket. She describes her husband as being “bemused by the whole thing”.

Dyer says she likes how Jellycat allows her to embrace her inner child. “They bring me a little bit of comfort, joy and escapism, and I don’t think there’s anything wrong with that, whatever your age.”

The Harrods brunch follows other Jellycat in-person experiences, including a patisserie in Galeries Lafayette in Paris that sells small plush chouquettes (small choux buns) and a ranch in Texas that features a bald-eagle soft toy called Algernon. When Selfridges first launched its Fish and Chips Jellycat van last July, people queued for up to three hours to buy characters including a plush sausage and mushy peas wrapped in a bespoke newspaper.

Jellycat’s revenue jumped by 43% on the previous year to £450m, October figures show.

Tang says in-person events where people can meet fellow collectors help form wider connections. “Shared interests give people an instant talking point,” she says. “That can be a huge anxiety soother for someone who may be lonely or shy to talk to people. Why should we question anything that builds community in these divided times?”

items.lbText:
Workers are sad but unsurprised as closures and job losses loom, while 2,000 suppliers will take a big hit

Poundland staff fear they’ll be left out in the cold for Christmas. When will workers have a say in their future?

“I feel Gordon Brothers punched us in the guts and took us down,” says Kelvin Blake, one of thousands of Poundland workers at risk of redundancy after the budget retailer’s US-based owners rejected at least two solvent bids for it.

While administrators at AlixPartners, who were appointed on Wednesday, continue to consider bids for the whole group, which has 600 stores in the UK and Ireland including the Dealz chain, more than 10,000 staff and thousands of suppliers face a grim Christmas of uncertainty.

The impact is being felt at Poundland stores across the country, as well at its head office and its distribution centres, including one in Andy Burnham’s Makerfield constituency.

Gordon Brothers, which bought Poundland last year for £1, has already collected close to £20m in interest payments and various fees, including those relating to store closures, according to documents provided to MPs. As a secured creditor on the majority of a £30m shareholder loan, Gordon Brothers is near the front of the queue to receive the proceeds of the administration including the sale of stock and store leases.

All stores currently remain open with about six main interested parties given until Sunday to put themselves in the bidding for Poundland now it is in administration. Those six potential bidders include: the Northern Irish company Martin Property Group; Zachert Private Equity, a German fund founded by a former Bloomberg journalist; little-known British fund Xyra Group Holdings; and Dubai’s Premier Quality Foods.

However, many industry watchers now expect the chain to be broken up, with significant job losses and store closures. Stocks are running low as the retailer is short of funds and many of its suppliers have stopped sending goods, fearing they will not be paid.

While trading had improved in recent months, it is understood that Poundland was not generating enough cash to cover its requirements and would need considerable funds to support its continued operation.

Blake, who has worked on the shop floor of one of Poundland’s Birmingham stores for 25 years, says the news has “put a downer on Christmas” but adds that he is “more worried about the future”. Now in his early 60s, he reckons it will be impossible to find another full-time contract with another retailer if his store does not remain open.

He says the administration – after Gordon Brothers rejected at least two solvent offers for the retailer and said it would not provide further funding to keep Poundland afloat – came despite a massive staff effort to turn the business around.

“The number of people coming through the doors was increasing day by day,” he said. “My store is a strong store.”

However, several other workers said that they felt the collapse of Poundland was inevitable.

“We knew at some point this was probably going to happen,” said one, who added the prospect of the store closing was “kind of worrying” but he hoped a potential buyer such as Tesco or the owner of Poundstretcher might snap up stores.

Referring to Gordon Brothers, he said: “They are doing everything legally right but not ethically right. Nobody can stop them.”

Reports this week that Poundstretcher’s US owners are lining up a sale suggest it is unlikely to rescue Poundland, though.

It is not only workers in stores that are affected. Hundreds of people work at Poundland’s two distribution centres in Bryn near Wigan and at Harlow in Essex, as well as at the head office in Walsall, near Birmingham.

Nearly 300 people are understood to work at Poundland’s eight-hectare (19-acre) site in the former coal mining village of Bryn in Ashton-in-Makerfield, within the prime minister’s constituency. It opened in 2018, and is one of the biggest retail employers in the area.

Jo Welbourne, a regional organiser for the Usdaw union, said staff are “absolutely devastated”, as many have worked at the site for a long time and live locally. “It’s devastating at any time of year but particularly around Christmas.”

A spokesperson for Gordon Brothers said: “Our thoughts are with Poundland colleagues. We recognise how difficult the continued uncertainty is for them. Efforts to preserve as many jobs and stores as possible will continue, led by the administrators.”

The spokesperson said Poundland had “faced several years of instability” and Gordon Brothers had provided £85m in new finance “stepping in when no one else was willing to finance the business”.

Still, about 2,000 suppliers will take a considerable hit as many have supplied stock which they will not be paid for and also have further money tied up in stocks or components to make items that they expected Poundland to buy.

Davey Martens, at independent confectionery supplier Byxa, said he was owed £68,515.20 by Poundland for products already supplied. Byxa’s future would be at risk if it cannot recover “a meaningful amount” of the money owed, he added.

“This might not sound like an enormous amount,” Martens said “But for a business like ours, it is. We can’t simply absorb a loss of this size and carry on as though nothing has happened. The consequences could be devastating.

Another supplier said he was owed more than $1.2m (£915,000) for clothing items already in stores or stuck in port in the UK. He said like many other suppliers, he accepted a switch to longer payment terms of 120 days from 90 days, in the interest of helping Poundland, before Gordon Brothers said it wanted to sell the business.

The supplier is having to pay for storage in the port as Poundland does not have the funds to enable the release of the goods despite them selling well in stores.

“That is the part that is frustrating and upsetting – the small guys end up losing while big corporations make money,” he said.…

items.lbText:
Papa John’s order was made without sharing bank security details – tech that could revolutionise shopping

Retailers enter the unknown with AI shopping assistants on Black Friday

An order of Papa John’s margherita pizzas has become the first purchase in the UK to be made using an AI agent using cardless payment technology.

The order of nine mini pizzas was made as part of the Financial Conduct Authority’s (FCA) regulated sandbox trials to test the technology, using Lloyds Bank and payment specialist TrueLayer.

London-based TrueLayer, which enables payments to be made between bank accounts without using cards, said it was the first time an AI agent had been used to pay a UK retailer for an order for a real customer.

“We completed this payment transaction with Papa John’s with no account numbers, no password [and] handled with the highest possible security profile,” said the TrueLayer chief executive, Francesco Simoneschi, in an interview with BBC Radio 4’s Today programme. “We talked with the AI agent, described the occasion and dietary requirements. Of course the agent suggested different flavours and quantities. We confirmed the order and the pizza arrived later.”

The team ordered the pizzas using the Papa John’s AI agent, which had been given permission to access their bank account and request payment to the retailer’s account.

Papa John’s AI agent was set to work with a strict mandate set with Lloyds, including a maximum spend limit per transaction and per month, with no account security information shared.

Simoneschi said the test was the first step toward mass adoption by the public of a technology that would fundamentally change purchasing habits.

“This is possibly the last Black Friday as we know it,” he said, referring to the annual online sales discount day. “At the moment plenty of us are already using AI to write up the shopping list. I think next year the agent will buy gifts on our behalf. Agents will do shopping on our behalf, will manage our finances, and will help us understand and compare complex products. This idea that they can really help us to sort out a lot of different aspects of our lives is a little bit like having an assistant available to millions of consumers out there.”

However, Simoneschi said consumers would still need to make informed decisions about how they used AI agents for making purchases.

“I think good [personal] judgment still applies, of course,” he said. “It does require control and supervision, and we need to make sure that the underlying technology is fit for purpose, while enforcing the highest possible security standards.”

He added that if there was an error or mistake in the order process, such as the agent ordering the wrong product, consumers would still be protected by existing rules and regulations covering buyers’ rights.

Earlier this week the FCA issued a warning to financial services companies developing AI agents that they must comply with existing regulations .

“The reason we are testing with regulators in this sandbox is to really understand all the aspects of the technology ahead of its mass adoption,” he said. “This is a great place to start.”

Meta’s personal AI assistant, Muse, which launched in the UK on Tuesday, can also make purchases online . Unlike TrueLayer, Muse makes payments using a customer’s bank card.
